slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open the lecture by positioning Chapter 6 as the coordinate chapter for noncompact symmetric spaces. The audience already knows symmetric pairs and rank; now the point is that negative-curvature geometry and semisimple algebra cooperate to make global decompositions possible. Keep the roadmap visible because Cartan, maximal compact, Iwasawa, nilpotent, and solvable viewpoints are the same space seen through different coordinates.

slides.title: Cartan Split
slides.notes: Present the Cartan decomposition as the first global-coordinate theorem, not as a bookkeeping split of the Lie algebra. In compact geometry an exponential chart can fold back on itself, but the noncompact model removes that obstruction. The proof thread uses the involution, the Killing-form sign pattern, and the convexity of geodesic distance to turn p0 into a complete coordinate plane for G/K.

slides.title: SL2 Model
slides.notes: Use the upper half-plane model to slow down the abstract theorem. A point of p0 is a tangent vector at the base coset, but exponentiating it lands at an actual point of the symmetric space. In the SL(2,R) model, that point has positive imaginary part, so the abstract Exp diffeomorphism becomes a concrete coordinate chart on familiar hyperbolic geometry.

slides.title: Maximal Compact
slides.notes: Frame this result as a geometric replacement for choosing K by hand. A compact subgroup acting on a noncompact symmetric space cannot drift forever; it has a fixed point. Once that point is moved to the base point, the subgroup becomes part of the isotropy group K. This is the bridge from global geometry to the conjugacy theorem for maximal compact subgroups.

slides.title: Iwasawa
slides.notes: Introduce Iwasawa decomposition as the chapter's main coordinate engine. The K part remembers a compact frame, A carries the flat rank directions, and N carries the positive restricted-root directions. The important point is global uniqueness: this is not a local triangularization near the identity but an analytic product description of every group element.

slides.title: SL2 KAN
slides.notes: Use the numerical table as a disciplined sanity check rather than a computational detour. In SL(2,R), Iwasawa decomposition has the same flavor as Gram-Schmidt: the first column determines a rotation and a positive length, and the remaining shear becomes N. The visual point is that A changes height while N moves along horocycle-like directions in the upper half-plane.

slides.title: Restricted Roots
slides.notes: Explain that N is not an arbitrary unipotent subgroup bolted onto the decomposition. It is built from the positive restricted-root spaces determined by the maximal abelian subspace a. In the split sl(3,R) example, those spaces are the strictly upper-triangular entries, and the bracket relation from E12 and E23 to E13 shows why the sum is nilpotent but usually not abelian.

slides.title: Nilpotent Lie Algebra
slides.notes: Pause here because nilpotence is the reason N is computationally friendly. In root coordinates, repeated commutators eventually move beyond the available positive roots, so the descending bracket series stops. That is what lets exponential coordinates on N have polynomial multiplication laws. The warning is that polynomial does not mean commutative; bracket corrections still carry real geometric information.

slides.title: BCH
slides.notes: Use the Heisenberg group as the cleanest way to see the nilpotent theorem in action. The first two coordinates add like ordinary translations, but the central coordinate receives a half-area correction. This correction is exactly the bracket term that survives in the truncated Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula, so the example ties algebra, geometry, and computation together.

slides.title: Global KAN
slides.notes: This slide should make the quotient logic explicit. KAN is a coordinate system on the group, but the symmetric space is G modulo K. After quotienting, the compact frame disappears and the remaining AN factor gives a global solvable model. This is the structural reason noncompact symmetric spaces can be studied through solvable Lie groups without losing points.

slides.title: Positive Symmetric
slides.notes: Connect the solvable model to a familiar matrix target. In the SL(2,R) realization, taking theta of s and multiplying by s inverse produces positive symmetric determinant-one matrices. The table turns three abstract adjectives into checks: symmetry residual zero, determinant one, and positive eigenvalues. This is a useful way to keep global decomposition from feeling purely formal.

slides.title: Complex Case
slides.notes: Treat the complex case as a change of scalars, not as a completely new phenomenon. When a complex semisimple Lie algebra is regarded as a real Lie algebra, the compact real form, the imaginary a direction, and the positive complex root spaces supply the Iwasawa pieces. The dimension count for sl(2,C) makes the multiplicity shift concrete and prevents students from undercounting n plus.

slides.title: Proof Roadmap
slides.notes: Use this dependency map either before proving the theorem or as a review after the examples. The algebraic side supplies the involution, the a-space, and the root spaces. The geometric side supplies the fixed-point interpretation of compact subgroups. The analytic side supplies global exponential behavior and nilpotent polynomial coordinates. Iwasawa decomposition sits at the meeting point of these ingredients.

slides.title: Misreadings
slides.notes: This slide is a useful checkpoint before assigning problems. Students often remember the letters K, A, and N but blur their roles. K is compact isotropy, A is a chosen flat direction, and N is built from positive restricted roots. The strongest correction is to tie each factor to an invariant or computation rather than to a visual mnemonic alone.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the central contrast: noncompact type gives global coordinates where compact type will later introduce periodicity, Weyl group identifications, and conjugate-point behavior. Students should leave with three linked formulas in mind: Cartan exponential coordinates on G/K, Iwasawa coordinates on G, and the solvable AN model after quotienting by K.
